summary.text: A 3-year-and-5-month-old boy, one of twins, developed neck pain and limited mobility ten days before admission, with no obvious predisposing factors, then gradual weakness of the right upper limb progressing to the right lower limb and abnormal gait. He had a history of minor neck trauma before onset. Physical examination upon admission found him conscious; recorded muscle strength was grade 1 in the right upper limb and grade 3 in the right lower limb, with normal left limb function and a forced position owing to pain.

Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging showed a cystic lesion with low T1 and high T2 signal on the ventral side of the spinal canal at cervical vertebra 2 to 4, compressing the spinal cord without obvious enhancement. Electromyography and somatosensory evoked potentials indicated impaired function of the high cervical spinal cord. The preoperative diagnosis was a cervical spinal canal space-occupying lesion, considered an enterogenous cyst, with spinal cord embolism.

Under general anesthesia the child underwent subdural lesion resection, cerebrospinal fluid leak repair and spinal canal plasty. Under the microscope the cyst was dissected along the ventral side of the spinal cord, its fluid was slightly turbid and its wall intact, and it was completely resected. The lamina was repositioned and the canal reconstructed. He went to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit and, after extubation, to the general ward.

Postoperative pathology was consistent with a neuroenteric cyst, and imaging on the second day after the operation showed complete resection and satisfactory decompression. Neurological function recovered well. At discharge, right upper limb strength was 3+, right lower limb strength 4+, and the pain was significantly relieved.

caption_evidence.quote:
Figure 2.
Results of preoperative electromyogram and evoked potential examinations. Motor nerve conduction examination revealed abnormalities in the amplitudes of nerve conduction and F-wave responses in the upper and lower limbs. The results of somatosensory evoked potential showed that the latency of bilateral Ninth Negative Peak was normal, but the latency of bilateral Thirteenth Negative Peak and Twentieth Negative Peak waves was prolonged, and the amplitudes were reduced, suggesting a conduction disorder at the level of the cervical spinal cord. A comprehensive judgment is consistent with the manifestations of high cervical spinal cord injury.
